guide.summary: Unit 5 covers how humans use land and water to produce food, timber, minerals, and living space, and the consequences: the tragedy of the commons, forestry practices, the Green Revolution, agricultural impacts, irrigation, pest control, meat production, fishing, mining, urbanization, ecological footprints, and sustainable alternatives. Expect solution-and-trade-off questions and water-use calculations.

sections.heading: Commons, forestry, and agriculture
sections.body: The tragedy of the commons occurs when individuals overuse a shared, unregulated resource (open-ocean fisheries, groundwater, air) because each gains the full benefit of use while costs are shared. Clearcutting removes all trees at once: cheap and efficient but increases erosion, raises stream temperatures, and destroys habitat; selective cutting and shelterwood cutting are more sustainable. The Green Revolution raised yields with high-yield crop varieties, synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation, and mechanization, but increased fossil-fuel use, monocultures with low genetic diversity, and nutrient runoff. Tilling increases erosion; slash-and-burn clears land quickly but depletes nutrients; synthetic fertilizer runoff causes eutrophication.

sections.heading: Irrigation and pest control
sections.body: Agriculture is the largest human use of fresh water. Furrow and flood irrigation are cheap but lose much water to evaporation and runoff; spray systems are moderately efficient; drip irrigation delivers water to roots and is the most efficient (over 90%) but is costly. Overwatering in arid regions causes waterlogging, and evaporation leaves salts behind (salinization). Pumping groundwater faster than recharge lowers the water table and can cause cones of depression and land subsidence; along coasts it can draw in salt water. Pesticides can kill nontarget species and select for resistant pests (the pesticide treadmill). Integrated pest management (IPM) combines biological controls, crop rotation, intercropping, and limited targeted chemical use.

sections.heading: Meat, fishing, and mining
sections.body: Concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) produce meat efficiently on little land but concentrate manure that can contaminate water with nitrates and pathogens, and require antibiotics and grain feed. Free-range grazing spreads manure naturally but uses more land and can cause overgrazing and desertification. Overfishing reduces fish size and can collapse fisheries; bottom trawling destroys seafloor habitat and causes bycatch. Aquaculture uses little space and fuel but can spread disease and waste to wild populations. Surface mining removes overburden and destroys habitat; mine tailings and exposed sulfides produce acid mine drainage that carries heavy metals into streams. Subsurface mining is more dangerous for workers and more costly but disturbs less land.

sections.heading: Urbanization and sustainability
sections.body: Urbanization increases impervious surfaces, which increases runoff and flooding and reduces groundwater recharge; it also creates heat islands and can increase sprawl. Urban runoff can be reduced with permeable pavement, rain gardens, green roofs, and public transit that slows sprawl. An ecological footprint measures the land and water area needed to supply a population's resources and absorb its wastes; a carbon footprint measures greenhouse gas emissions. Sustainable practices include contour plowing, terracing, windbreaks, perennial crops, no-till agriculture, cover crops, rotational grazing, and sustainable forestry (reforestation, selective cutting, using fire management).

sections.heading: Worked example: irrigation and water use
sections.body: Agriculture uses roughly 70% of global fresh water withdrawals. Flood irrigation is inexpensive but inefficient, with much water lost to evaporation and runoff, and it can cause waterlogging and soil salinization. Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots and can exceed 90% efficiency, though it costs more to install. Overpumping aquifers can lower water tables, cause land subsidence, and allow saltwater intrusion near coasts.

sections.heading: Sustainable practices
sections.body: Sustainable agriculture includes crop rotation, intercropping, contour plowing, terracing, no-till farming, windbreaks, and integrated pest management, which combines biological controls, crop rotation, and limited pesticide use. Sustainable forestry uses selective cutting, replanting, and protection of old-growth forests. Urban sustainability measures include public transit, green roofs, and permeable pavement to reduce runoff.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students often describe impacts without explaining the mechanism, such as saying monocultures are bad without explaining reduced biodiversity, increased pest vulnerability, and soil nutrient depletion.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know tragedy of the commons, clear-cutting, slash-and-burn, Green Revolution, monoculture, salinization, IPM, CAFOs, overfishing, bycatch, mining types, urban sprawl, and ecological footprint.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Free-response questions often ask you to identify an environmental problem from agriculture, forestry, fishing, or mining and propose a specific solution with an explanation of how it works. A strong answer names the solution and its mechanism, such as 'contour plowing reduces soil erosion by slowing water runoff across slopes.'

keyTakeaways: Shared, unregulated resources tend to be overused.
Drip irrigation is most efficient; flood and furrow lose the most water.
Irrigation in arid areas causes salinization.
IPM reduces pesticide use and resistance.
Impervious surfaces increase runoff and flooding.
Every solution has a trade-off; name both sides.
commonMistakes: Saying the tragedy of the commons applies to privately owned land.
Claiming aquaculture has no environmental impacts.
Forgetting that pesticides select for resistance rather than causing mutations.
Giving vague solutions like 'farm sustainably' without a specific practice.
examTips: Solutions questions want a specific practice plus how it works.
Know at least one advantage and one disadvantage for each farming, fishing, and mining method.
Water-use calculations often compare irrigation efficiencies; set up as volume needed ÷ efficiency.
Footprint questions compare per-capita demand to available biocapacity.
guide.cramSheet:
**Commons:** shared + unregulated → overuse · fix: quotas, permits, ownership

**Forestry:** clearcut cheap, erosion, warmer streams · selective/shelterwood better

**Green Revolution:** HYVs, fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation, machines · monoculture, runoff

**Irrigation:** drip > spray > flood/furrow · salinization · aquifer depletion

**Pests:** treadmill · IPM: biocontrol, rotation, intercropping

**Meat:** CAFO efficient land use, concentrated waste · free range more land

**Fish:** overfishing, bycatch, trawling · aquaculture: disease, waste

**Mining:** overburden · acid mine drainage

**Urban:** impervious → runoff · permeable pavement, rain gardens, green roofs

vocab.definition: Overuse of a shared resource because individuals act in their own interest.
Removing all trees in an area at once.
Mid-20th-century shift to high-yield crops, synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation, and mechanization.
Growing a single crop over a large area.
Buildup of salts in soil from irrigation water evaporating in arid areas.
Delivery of water directly to plant roots through perforated tubing; highly efficient.
A combination of biological, physical, and limited chemical methods to control pests.
Concentrated animal feeding operation: large numbers of animals raised in confined spaces.
Soil and rock removed to reach a mineral deposit in surface mining.
A surface such as pavement that water cannot penetrate.
Area of land and water needed to supply resources and absorb wastes for a person or population.

practice.stem: Which situation best illustrates the tragedy of the commons?

choices.text: Many fishing fleets harvest an unregulated international fish stock until it collapses.
A farmer rotates crops on her own land to maintain soil fertility.
A city builds a reservoir for its residents.
A company replants trees on land it owns after harvesting.

practice.explanation: Each fleet gains by catching more, while the cost of depletion is shared by all.

distractors.B: Private land with incentive to conserve.

practice.stem: Which irrigation method delivers the highest percentage of applied water to plant roots?

choices.text: Flood irrigation
Drip irrigation
Spray irrigation
Furrow irrigation

practice.explanation: Drip systems release water slowly at the root zone, minimizing evaporation and runoff.

practice.stem: Which practice is part of integrated pest management?

choices.text: Spraying broad-spectrum insecticide on a fixed weekly schedule
Planting one crop variety across the entire farm
Releasing ladybugs to eat aphids and rotating crops each year
Doubling pesticide doses when pests return

practice.explanation: IPM relies on biological control and cultural practices, using chemicals only when needed.

practice.stem: Which was a major disadvantage of the Green Revolution?

choices.text: Crop yields decreased worldwide.
It reduced irrigation use.
It increased crop genetic diversity.
It increased dependence on fossil fuels for fertilizer, pesticides, and machinery.

practice.explanation: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer production and mechanization depend heavily on fossil fuels.

practice.stem: A field's crops need 600,000 L of water to reach their roots. Furrow irrigation is 65% efficient and drip irrigation is 95% efficient. Approximately how much water would switching from furrow to drip save?
In a hot, arid valley irrigated for decades, crop yields are falling and white crusts appear on the soil surface. The most likely cause is

choices.text: nitrogen fixation by crops
acid deposition from nearby power plants
salinization from evaporation of irrigation water that leaves dissolved salts behind
an increase in soil organic matter

practice.explanation: Irrigation water contains small amounts of salt; high evaporation concentrates it at the surface.

practice.stem: Which change to a city parking lot would most reduce storm-water runoff?

choices.text: Replacing it with permeable pavement and adding a vegetated rain garden at its low edge
Resurfacing it with new asphalt
Adding more storm drains that lead to a river
Painting it white to reduce heat

practice.explanation: Permeable surfaces and rain gardens let water infiltrate instead of running off.

distractors.C: Moves runoff faster rather than reducing it.

practice.stem: Clearcutting a forest along a trout stream is most likely to harm the trout by

choices.text: increasing shade and lowering water temperature
reducing the amount of rain reaching the stream
adding dissolved oxygen to the stream
removing shade, warming the water, and increasing sediment that covers spawning gravel

practice.explanation: Warmer water holds less oxygen, and eroded sediment smothers eggs.

practice.stimulus: Over 40 years, the average length of cod caught in a fishery fell from 90 cm to 50 cm, and the age at which cod first reproduce fell from 6 years to 4 years, while total catch steadily declined.

choices.text: The fishery is sustainable because cod are still being caught.
The fish population is healthier because cod reproduce earlier.
Warmer water caused cod to grow larger.
Heavy fishing removed the largest, oldest fish, shifting the population toward smaller, earlier-maturing individuals and signaling overfishing.

practice.explanation: Size-selective harvest removes large fish; declining catch and size both indicate an overexploited stock.

practice.stem: Which is a disadvantage of raising salmon in open-net pens along a coast?

choices.text: Waste, parasites, and disease from crowded pens can spread to wild fish nearby.
It requires more fuel than catching wild salmon.
It needs more land than wild fishing.
It increases bycatch of dolphins.

practice.explanation: High densities concentrate waste and pathogens such as sea lice, which escape into surrounding water.

practice.stem: Streams below an abandoned coal mine have a pH of 3.5 and orange deposits. Which process most likely explains this?

choices.text: Fertilizer runoff from nearby farms lowered the pH.
Coal dust neutralizes the stream.
Exposed sulfide minerals react with water and oxygen to form sulfuric acid, which dissolves metals such as iron.
Thermal pollution from the mine raised water temperature.

practice.explanation: Acid mine drainage forms when sulfides oxidize; dissolved iron precipitates as orange iron hydroxides.

practice.stimulus: A farm applied the same insecticide each season. In year 1, it killed 95% of a beetle pest; by year 6, it killed 40%.

choices.text: Individual beetles developed immunity after being sprayed.
Beetles that survived because of heritable resistance reproduced, so resistance became more common each generation.
The insecticide was mutated by sunlight.
The beetles migrated away from the farm.

practice.explanation: Pesticides select for existing resistant individuals; resistance increases through natural selection.

distractors.A: Individuals don't acquire heritable resistance by exposure.

practice.stimulus: Country Q has 20 million people, an average ecological footprint of 5.0 global hectares (gha) per person, and total biocapacity of 40 million gha.

choices.text: Country Q has an ecological reserve of 60 million gha.
Country Q uses 2.5 times its biocapacity, an ecological deficit of 60 million gha.
Country Q's footprint equals its biocapacity.
Country Q uses 40% of its biocapacity.

practice.explanation: Footprint = 20 million × 5.0 = 100 million gha; 100/40 = 2.5; deficit = 60 million gha.

practice.stem: Which pairing correctly gives an advantage and a disadvantage of CAFOs compared with free-range grazing?

choices.text: Advantage: no grain feed required; disadvantage: higher prices
Advantage: no antibiotics needed; disadvantage: more land per unit of meat
Advantage: manure is spread naturally; disadvantage: overgrazing
Advantage: less land per unit of meat; disadvantage: concentrated manure that can contaminate water with nitrates and pathogens

practice.explanation: Confinement saves land but concentrates waste in lagoons that can leak or overflow.

practice.frqType: Q2 Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution
practice.prompt: In a semi-arid farming region, center-pivot sprinklers pump water from an aquifer to grow corn and cotton. Over 50 years, the water table has dropped 30 meters, several shallow wells have gone dry, and some fields near the edge of the region show declining yields and white salt deposits. Average annual recharge of the aquifer is far smaller than the annual withdrawal.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how the data show that the aquifer is being used unsustainably.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the tragedy of the commons applies to this aquifer.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how irrigation causes the white salt deposits and declining yields.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Describe one consequence, other than dry wells, of continued groundwater overdraft.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Propose one solution that would reduce aquifer depletion, and explain how it reduces withdrawal.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Describe one economic disadvantage of your solution for farmers.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Identify one crop choice change that would reduce water demand and explain why.

rubric.description: Withdrawal exceeds recharge, shown by the 30 m drop in the water table.
Many farmers draw from one aquifer that no individual owns or controls.
Each farmer benefits from pumping more, while the cost (a lower water table) is shared by all, so total use exceeds sustainable levels.
Irrigation water contains dissolved salts; in hot, dry conditions water evaporates and salts remain in the soil.
Salt buildup makes it harder for roots to absorb water (osmotic stress), reducing yields.
E.g., land subsidence, higher pumping costs and energy use, reduced stream base flow, wetland loss.
E.g., convert to drip irrigation, install meters with pumping limits or water pricing, schedule irrigation using soil-moisture sensors.
Explains how the solution delivers needed water with less loss or caps total withdrawal below recharge.
E.g., high installation cost of drip systems; reduced income from smaller irrigated area; cost of meters or water fees.
E.g., switch to drought-tolerant crops such as sorghum or wheat, which need less water than corn or cotton.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The water table has dropped 30 meters because withdrawals far exceed natural recharge, so water is being removed faster than it is replaced.

(b) The aquifer is a shared resource that no single farmer controls. Each farmer gains the full benefit of pumping more water, while the cost of the falling water table is spread among everyone, so all farmers over-pump and the aquifer is depleted.

(c) Irrigation water carries small amounts of dissolved salt. In the hot, semi-arid climate, water evaporates from the soil surface and leaves the salts behind. Over time the salt concentration rises, making it harder for roots to take up water, so crop yields fall.

(d) As water is removed, sediments in the aquifer compact, causing land subsidence that can damage roads and buildings.

(e) Convert from center-pivot sprinklers to drip irrigation. Drip lines deliver water directly to roots, so far less water is lost to evaporation and wind drift, and farmers can grow the same crop while pumping less groundwater.

(f) Drip systems are expensive to buy and install, which may be difficult for small farms to afford.

(g) Switch from corn to sorghum, which is drought-tolerant and needs considerably less water per growing season.
